The Central Bank has flagged agriculture as one of the sectors facing the most severe labor shortages heading toward 2030.

risks: Black Sea shipping and insurance disruptions from the war
Export quota and taxation policy volatility
Worsening farm labor shortages
opportunities: Growing grain trade with China and Asian markets
Strong 2025/26 harvest supporting export volumes

shortTerm.summary: Independent analysis (Re:Russia) finds the Russian IT sector's growth under forced import substitution has largely translated into higher prices rather than a genuine capacity breakthrough. A separate report noted that companies spent 116 times more implementing import-substitute IT solutions than the 1.6 billion rubles in benefits gained, suggesting inefficiency in the transition. Adjacent segments show robust nominal growth: the telecom-adjacent Big Data & AI market grew to an estimated 433 billion rubles in 2024 and a projected 520 billion rubles in 2025 (~20% growth), per TAdviser/Association of Big Data/B1 research.

longTerm.summary: Growth continues to be driven by government support, import-substitution mandates, and cloud-infrastructure expansion, but structural constraints persist: a shortage of machine-learning and other specialists, and a market structure oriented toward selling anonymized analytical reports and packaged solutions rather than raw data due to stringent storage/processing regulations, which raises costs relative to more open markets.

risks: Import-substitution mandates driving costs up without proportional capability gains
Continued loss of access to Western software and cloud platforms
Shortage of qualified IT/ML specialists
opportunities: Government-mandated demand for domestic software vendors
Rapid growth of the domestic Big Data and AI services market

shortTerm.summary: Russia has acknowledged failure of its electronics import-substitution program, per Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service reporting on Russian government data: the 2030 domestic-content target was cut from 80% to 58.7%, program funding will fall from $338.4 million (2024) to $62.6 million (2026), and deadlines for domestic processors/modems were pushed to 2032. Russia's touted 'Irtysh' processor was found to be a copy of a Chinese Loongson chip.

longTerm.summary: Russian experts cited in the same reporting acknowledge the country lacks a full production cycle for modern electronics (materials, equipment, and technology), and that localization above 60% is impossible without domestic 28nm-or-smaller chip fabrication, which sanctions currently block — implying continued structural dependence on imports (increasingly from China) over the long term.

risks: Lack of domestic advanced chip fabrication capability under sanctions
Sharp cuts to electronics import-substitution program funding
Delayed processor/modem production deadlines (pushed to 2032)
opportunities: Continued reliance on Chinese semiconductor and electronics supply as a stopgap

shortTerm.summary: Per TAdviser, the 30 largest Russian robot manufacturers earned 29.3 billion rubles in 2023, up 44.3% from 20.3 billion rubles in 2022, with over 460 companies now active in service robotics across 21 segments as of October 2024. Robot density reached 11 robots per 10,000 workers, up from 6 four years earlier — growing faster than the global average, though Russia still holds only about 0.2% of the global industrial robot stock (7,000-7,500 units vs. 3.5 million worldwide).

longTerm.summary: The government has allocated 300 billion rubles toward robotization through 2030, including subsidies covering up to 50% of robot purchase costs and a new National Anthropomorphic Platform for humanoid robot development (Sberbank unveiled its humanoid robot 'Green' in November 2025). Structural constraints remain significant: an estimated 30,000 robotics specialists are needed annually, 58.8% of Russian robotics firms don't export, and 76.5% of firms are still in an early commercialization stage.

risks: Severe shortage of qualified robotics specialists (~30,000/year needed)
Very low robot density and manufacturing base relative to global leaders
Most firms still pre-commercial, limiting near-term export potential
opportunities: Large state funding commitment (300 billion rubles through 2030) and purchase subsidies
Fast-growing service robotics segment (460+ companies, 21 segments)
